claims.text: Maximized configurational entropy produces a highly disordered, broad valence band in noble-metal HEA nanoparticles.
A broad valence-band spectrum and random atomic configurations correspond to a variety of local electronic structures.
The electronic disorder creates a variety of near-degenerate catalytic active sites.
Atomic-scale randomness enhances charge-transfer kinetics.
Atomic-scale randomness enhances catalytic turnover.
Configurational entropy governs reliable formation of a homogeneous single-phase HEA nanoparticle.
A one-pot polyol process can synthesize nanoparticles containing Ru, Rh, Pd, Ir, and Pt as an HEA.
The one-pot polyol process effectively maintains atomic-level homogeneity and avoids elemental segregation.
A random atomic configuration yields a broad, featureless valence-band spectrum.
Atomic-scale randomness produces a continuum of catalytic active-site energies.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the disordered electronic structure.
Multiple energetically similar active sites improve electron distribution.
Faster charge transfer caused by electronic disorder enhances HER activity.
The HEA nanoparticles will have a lower HER overpotential than a conventional Pt catalyst.
The HEA nanoparticles will have a significantly higher HER turnover frequency than commercial Pt at low overpotential in both acidic and alkaline electrolytes.
The HEA nanoparticles will have superior cyclic stability to commercial Pt in both acidic and alkaline electrolytes.
Conventional Pt catalysts have a narrow, more defined d-band structure.
Conventional Pt catalysts have fewer active sites because their atomic arrangements are more uniform.
The proposed mechanism applies to aqueous electrocatalysis at ambient temperature when atomic-level homogeneity is maintained.
Elemental segregation or clustering compromises the proposed electronic-disorder mechanism and its catalytic benefit.
